extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of moral/philosophical essays; readers of Montaigne (translated 1877)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of personal-philosophical essays (Montaigne) giving normative guidance and reflections on courage, constancy, fear, courtesy, ambassadorship, obedience, punishment, superstition, and the judgment of happiness. The text mixes illustrative anecdotes, classical quotations, and practical maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of divination and almanacs
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat belief in almanacs and prophetic writings with skepticism: accidental 'hits' are to be expected among infinite false prognostics and do not validate the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'I see some who are mightily given to study and comment upon their almanacs... it is hardly possible but that these alleged authorities sometimes stumble upon a truth amongst an infinite number of lies.' He notes that false predictions are not recorded, and that prophetic writings are often obscure and ambiguous so posterity can interpret them to fit events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of sudden moral impulses in cultivated souls
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow some authority to sudden, vehement, and fortuitous promptings of the will in persons whose minds are enlightened and prepared by exercise of wisdom and virtue (the 'Socratic demon' or impulsion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests such prompt, undigested inclinations may be important and 'worthy to be followed' in souls disciplined by virtue; he reports having experienced similar prompt persuasions that proved advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy: bravely endure unavoidable harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Constancy requires bravely to stand to and stoutly to suffer those inconveniences which are not possibly to be avoided, while still using honest means to secure oneself from harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law of resolution and constancy does not forbid taking precautions or fearing threats, but is chiefly about enduring inevitable mischiefs; even awkward physical motions are acceptable if they protect from harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retreat and flight can be strategic
rubrics_metrics.description: Retreating or giving ground is not necessarily cowardice; it can be a legitimate and skilful tactic in war or other affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Turks retaining a flight practice, Homer commends AEneas's science of flight, Lacedaemonians used feigned flight at Plataea to break the enemy. Socrates (in Plato) ridicules defining fortitude as mere standing firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abandon post before inevitable artillery danger
rubrics_metrics.description: When danger (e.g., cannon-shot) is swift and inevitable, quitting a post to avoid it is unseemly and may be mocked; sudden evasions are often physical reflexes rather than judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes (Marquis de Guast, Lorenzo de' Medici) illustrate that ducking or slipping aside in face of sudden artillery may be fortuitous, not prudent deliberation; Montaigne doubts such evasions are acts of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic allowance for natural fear if judgment remains intact
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoics permit natural first impressions of fear (trembling, paleness, convulsion) provided the seat of reason suffers no alteration and judgment remains sound and consenting is withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with non-philosophers whose passions penetrate to reason and corrupt judgment. Quoted verse: 'Mens immota manet; lachrymae volvuntur inanes.' Peripatetics also do not entirely exempt from perturbation but moderate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy: necessary but not enslaving to ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of courtesy and good manners is necessary—like grace and beauty they beget liking—but one should not be servilely enslaved to ceremonies to the detriment of personal liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne values following civilities but prefers offending someone once rather than enslaving himself to perpetual observance; excesses of over-politeness can be rude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassadors must report the whole truth to their sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: An ambassador's duty is to represent faithfully the whole of what occurred to his master, not to conceal or disguise important facts on account of fearing the master's reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes ambassadors who omitted offensive or provocative statements from Charles V in reports to their king; he argues the sovereign must retain liberty of judgment and decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambassadors require discretion and initiative within their remit
rubrics_metrics.description: Though ambassadors owe obedience, their employment is not strictly confined; many matters are referred to their own discretion and they must form and model their master's pleasure by active judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaignes notes the harm of giving lieutenants too little rein (e.g., Persian kings' practice) and praises ambassadors who exercise appropriate independence in vast dominions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to positive commands versus professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit and precise obedience is due to explicit, positive orders; this discipline can be valued even over technical correctness in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: Crassus whipped an engineer who disregarded direct order even though his technical choice was more appropriate—discipline and office integrity sometimes trump technical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour has bounds; obstinacy in untenable defence is punishable
rubrics_metrics.description: Valour can become vice when excessive; those who obstinately defend a fort that is not defensible may be justly punished to prevent ruinous consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne explains why laws punish obstinate defenders (examples: siege punishments) — to deter needless resistance that would jeopardize many and encourage disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish cowardice from infirmity; prefer shame over death for cowardice
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate faults proceeding from natural infirmity from those born of treachery; for many such infirmities the law and custom (Charondas) used ignominy and shame rather than death, aiming to awaken courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roman and Greek practices varied; Montaigne recounts public exposure in woman's attire or degradation as punishments intended to stir courage rather than execute. Extreme ignorance or cowardice that appears treacherous, however, may warrant severe punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear undermines judgment; 'fear of fear' is worst
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is the passion that most quickly dethrones judgment and can be more tormenting than death; fear spreads, causes madness, or immobilizes and can push people to desperate acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous historical anecdotes (soldiers mistaking reeds for pikes, panic at Carthage, Roman defeats) illustrate fear's destructive effects. Montaigne: 'The thing in the world I am most afraid of is fear.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pronounce someone happy until after death
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot rightly call a person happy until he has passed his last day, because human fortune is mutable and any present prosperity may be overturned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Croesus and Solon's teaching: the final state after death determines true felicity; we should 'look forward to our last day.'
